reason: Quotes state AWS attaches a new inline policy denying all permissions to all actions and that only role credentials issued before the specified time become invalid; later sessions are outside that condition.

Quotes state the policy denies all permissions when aws:TokenIssueTime is earlier than the specified time and that the key exists only for temporary-credential requests, so IAM user long-term credentials are unaffected.

Quotes define role chaining, limit the session to one hour regardless of the role's maximum session duration, and exempt the initial assumption from user credentials and EC2 instance-profile applications.

Quotes support an optional account setting that provisions roles and roles that can be viewed, edited or deleted; 'using role templates' and 'supported service consoles' appear only in surrounding context, not in any quote.
Quote states the setting ranges from 1 hour to 12 hours, the default maximum of 1 hour applies when unset, and it does not limit sessions assumed by AWS services.

Quotes state the assumed role's permissions policy determines the permissions of credentials from AssumeRole, AssumeRoleWithSAML and AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity, and that the trust policy says who may assume the role.

Quotes state the IAM resource-based policy type is the role trust policy, its Principal element names who can assume the role, and the principals include accounts, users, roles, federated users and services.
Quote states IAM supports only one resource-based policy type, the role trust policy, a role needs both a trust policy and an identity-based policy, and trust policies define who can assume it.
Quotes state IAM Roles Anywhere extends IAM to on-premises and hybrid workloads with temporary credentials and the same roles and policies, and that it requires PKI.
Quotes state roles rely on temporary credentials, are not associated with a specific user or group, are assumed by trusted entities, and that short-term credentials are a security best practice.

Quote states that after centralizing root access you can remove member root credentials, new Organizations accounts have none by default, and member accounts cannot sign in as root or recover the password.
Quote recommends removing member root credentials, lists password, access keys, signing certificates and deleting MFA, and states member accounts cannot sign in as root or recover the password.
Quote strongly recommends not creating root access keys because root has full access to all services and resources including billing information.

Quote supports not sharing the listed root credentials except with a strict business need; 'use root credentials only for the tasks that require them' is in the preceding context sentence, not the quote.

Quotes support MFA for all account types, the 35-day window, and the May 2024 and June 2024 steps; the June 2025 date for member accounts is in no quote (only the page's 'Posted on: Jun 17, 2025' line).

Quote, read with its preceding sentence that defines 'these tasks', states short-term privileged sessions with temporary credentials scoped to specific actions, without root sign-in on the member account.
Quote lists exactly the four tasks: delete a misconfigured S3 bucket policy, delete a misconfigured SQS queue policy, delete and re-enable member root credentials.
Quote states standalone accounts need root credentials to close, while member accounts can be closed centrally from the management and delegated admin accounts.
Quote, under the heading of tasks that require root credentials, states you sign in as root to edit policies and restore permissions the only IAM administrator revoked.

Quote states standalone accounts need root credentials for email, root password and root access keys, while other account settings do not, which bounds the 'only' to account settings as the claim does.
Quotes state the listed tasks can be performed only when signed in as root, and the restore-administrator-permissions task is one of them.
Quote states the root user can be the principal in a resource-based policy and, in an organization member account, is affected by the account's SCPs and RCPs.
Quote states the root user is the most privileged user with full administrative access and in some cases cannot be constrained by security policies.
Quote states identity-based policies cannot be attached to the root user and a permissions boundary cannot be set for it.
Quote states root must not be used for everyday tasks even administrative ones, only for tasks that require it, with other actions done by users assuming roles.
Quote states S3 MFA Delete is for root account access only, is enabled with the bucket versioning state, cannot apply to an IAM user, and is managed independently of MFA-protected API access.
Quote states an SCP Allow grants no permission and SCPs act as filters setting maximum permissions for the accounts, which entails that an AdministratorAccess user is still limited.

Quotes support SCPs restricting IAM users and roles in member accounts including the root user, but not 'every' role: the same SCP page says SCPs do not affect service-linked roles and lists other exceptions.
Quotes state that with an SCP, a permissions boundary and an identity-based policy, all three must allow the request and effective permissions are their intersection.
Quotes state a Condition element can be used in SCP allow and deny statements and NotAction can exclude AWS services from the policy's effect.
Quote states SCPs use almost the same syntax as IAM policies but do not grant permissions.
Quote in the Organizations FAQ states a policy attaches to the organization root, an OU (all accounts including nested OUs), or individual accounts.
Quote states effective permissions in an account with an SCP are the intersection of what the SCP allows and what IAM permission policies grant.
Quote states an empty SCP does not allow all actions and is equivalent to a policy that explicitly denies all actions, as an empty policy is a default deny.
Quote gives the example of IAM allowing ec2 and sqs, SCP allowing ec2 and s3, and the result being only ec2.
Quote states principals in a member account, including its root user, cannot remove or change SCPs applied to that account.
Quote states the IAM policy simulator can include SCP effects and can be used in a member account to see the effect on individual principals.
Quote states SCPs allow or deny service access for individual member accounts or groups of accounts in an OU and affect all IAM users and roles including the member root user.
Quotes state SCPs set maximum permissions for users and roles in an organization or OU, limit identity- and resource-based grants, include each member root user, and grant nothing.
Quotes state SCPs and RCPs are not available with consolidated billing only, and SCPs apply when all features are enabled.
